video_title: Dan Ives on AI, Tesla, SpaceX, Coreweave, and more
gist: Dan Ives (Yorkville Ives) reports memory demand up about 30% in four to six weeks from his Korea trip and argues the AI sell-off (CoreWeave CDS, the KOSPI rout) is a narrative-driven 'SaaS apocalypse' moment. He says the Street underestimates tech earnings by 15-25%, targets 8,000 on the S&P, and sees no supply-demand equilibrium until 2029. He also puts 80-90% odds on a SpaceX-Tesla merger that would value Tesla at $500-550, and flags midterm and data-center moratorium risk.

themes.theme: Asia memory demand vs. AI-bear narrative

insights.claim: Dan Ives says memory chip demand he observed on the ground in Korea is up roughly 30% in the last four to six weeks, leaving him incrementally more bullish despite the AI-trade sell-off.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Channel checks point to accelerating memory demand while prices fell, a fundamentals-vs-sentiment gap.
insights.quote: memory if I look at demand it's probably up about 30% in the last four to six weeks

insights.claim: Ives argues the sharp KOSPI sell-off is detached from fundamentals, driven by leverage and a flood of retail traders into a market that was long ignored, and predicts the KOSPI makes new all-time highs going into next year.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Korean memory names may be oversold on positioning, not demand; a rebound trade setup.
insights.quote: I continue to believe like the Cosby will make new all-time highs

insights.claim: Ives points to Micron trading at roughly five times earnings and SK's dual listing in the US as signs memory is mispriced and that Korea's role in the AI trade will broaden beyond memory to neoclouds and software.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Memory equities trade at very low multiples relative to the demand story; US listing could widen the investor base.
insights.quote: Micron's training what five times earnings

insights.claim: The host notes that one to two Fridays before the recording, S&P put buying was the second-highest in history and Nasdaq the third-highest, a contrarian signal that marked the turning point of the panic.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano (host)
insights.so_what: Extreme hedging usually means positioning is washed out and short-covering fuels rallies.
insights.quote: the S&P put buying was second highest in history. NASDAQ third highest in history

insights.claim: Ives's validation framework is that Asian supply-chain demand is the real report card on AI, together with CIO checks showing enterprise use cases multiplying at companies like Palantir and Snowflake; he says US bears who never visit Taiwan or Korea miss this.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Supply-chain orders in Asia are a leading indicator to watch ahead of US earnings.

insights.claim: Ives says AI has moved from capex to monetization, with the gap between the two nearly over, and puts the cycle at less than 15% through, with no supply-demand equilibrium until 2029.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: If he is right, the earnings upcycle runs for years and dips are buying opportunities.
insights.quote: we're less and 15% through where we are and I believe like we don't have equilibrium till 2029

themes.theme: CoreWeave, neocloud debt and rate risk

insights.claim: Ives concedes the bears are directionally right that rising yields raise the cost of capital, since about 20% of the AI buildout must be funded with debt or converts/equity.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Debt-funded AI infrastructure names are the most rate-sensitive part of the trade.
insights.quote: about 20% of the buildout is going to either have to be debt funded

insights.claim: Ives argues CoreWeave's debt is minuscule relative to its backlog, and calls the infrastructure sell-off a 'SaaS apocalypse' style narrative moment rather than a fundamental break.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: He thinks CoreWeave CDS widening overstates credit risk relative to contracted revenue.
insights.quote: the debt that they're taking on relative to their backlog is minuscule

insights.claim: Ives names Oracle and CoreWeave as the poster children for taking on disproportionate debt to build AI capacity, notes Oracle's stock falling as the market dislikes debt-funded hyperscaling, and says the cash-rich hyperscalers are in a far better position.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Within AI infrastructure, how a company funds itself sorts the winners: the balance-sheet-funded hyperscalers over the levered builders.
insights.quote: Oracle and coreweave really being poster childs in terms of those two names taking on a lot of debt

insights.claim: Ives says rising rates come largely from the AI capex boom itself, and estimates a 50-75bp rise might affect only about 1% of data centers, so further Fed hikes would not significantly slow the buildout unless the 10-year goes much higher, Jimmy Carter style.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Only a severe rate spike threatens AI capex; small hikes are noise for the thesis.

insights.claim: Ives still believes the market needs more neoclouds because AI demand will exceed supply, cites Jensen Huang saying the same, and says he would bet against the negative neocloud narrative even after a small neocloud IPO fell 30%.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: A contrarian long setup in beaten-down neoclouds if capacity stays tight.
insights.quote: I still believe you need more Neoclouds

insights.claim: Ives claims every $1 of hyperscaler capex creates $5-6 of spending across the rest of tech, and on that basis says the Street is underestimating tech earnings by 15-25% over the next 12-18 months.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: He expects positive earnings revisions to drive the next leg up, not multiple expansion.
insights.quote: street is underestimating earnings 15 20 25% next 12 to 18 months

insights.claim: Ives reiterates an S&P 500 target of about 8,000 for this year, noting that six months earlier, with oil at $105-110 and the 10-year near 5% while the Fed was hiking, most would have guessed 6,500-6,800.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: A bullish index target that implies more upside even after rate hikes and an oil shock.

insights.claim: Ives rejects the 1999/fiber-bubble comparison because this buildout is funded by big tech with about a trillion dollars on balance sheets and $300-400B of annual free cash flow, and says tech now trades around 21 times earnings and is getting cheaper even as bearishness rises.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Capex funded from cash flow is less fragile than the debt-funded telecom buildout of the late 1990s.
insights.quote: Three to 400 billion a year of free cash flow

insights.claim: Asked about concentration (the top 15 S&P companies at 46% of index market value), Ives says it would only worry him if spending were not spreading, and predicts that within a year AI spending broadens to software, infrastructure, energy and cybersecurity.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Points toward rotation into second-derivative AI beneficiaries such as software, energy and cyber.

insights.claim: Ives argues Apple and Meta stocks are rerating because the market expects them to start monetizing consumer AI, with Meta narrowing the gap with Anthropic and OpenAI, and says Muse matters because it brings AI to mainstream consumers while physical AI has not even started.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Consumer AI monetization is the next catalyst for mega-cap platforms.

insights.claim: Ives puts the probability of a SpaceX-Tesla merger at 80-90%, saying it would take something anomalous to stop it, with special committees at both companies already reviewing it.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Prediction markets reportedly price it far lower (the host cites odds as low as 18-20%), a big gap for event-driven traders.

insights.claim: Ives believes a deal would value Tesla at roughly $500-550 per share, a 30-40% premium to the current $370-375, and he cannot see a deal happening below $500.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: This sets an implied deal-price target for Tesla stock as a merger-arb trade.
insights.quote: I couldn't see a deal happening sub $500

insights.claim: Ives's strategic case for the merger: Tesla's data would turbocharge SpaceX's push to become a hyperscaler, engineers could move between the companies, and Musk would hold all his AI technology under one roof. He adds that SpaceX trails Microsoft, Amazon and Alphabet as a hyperscaler, and that running two separate companies is hard for Musk.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: This reframes the combined company as a vertically integrated AI hyperscaler rather than as autos plus rockets.

insights.claim: Ives says the merger must happen during the Trump administration, giving a window of about 1.5-2 years, and expects heavy regulatory scrutiny over Tesla's China exposure combined with SpaceX's national-security role. The combined company would be worth $4-5 trillion, the largest merger in history.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: A political-timeline catalyst plus regulatory risk are the key variables for the deal.
insights.quote: it would have to be between four to 5 trillion

insights.claim: Ives reports that most hedge funds are expressing the trade by buying SpaceX on fundamentals, while he sees Tesla as the opportunity because it would rerate quickly once there is a concrete deal rather than just talk.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: How institutions are positioned shows which leg of the trade is crowded and which is lagging.
insights.quote: right now most are buying SpaceX

insights.claim: The host argues Tesla could run from about $370 to $420-450 on speculation into the decision point, so holders keep gains even if the deal fails, and says the merger may now be the number one reason to own Tesla.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano (host)
insights.so_what: This frames an asymmetric event-driven long into the announcement.

insights.claim: Ives says Tesla has underperformed this year because it is in an investment year moving from EV maker to AI player (Optimus, autonomy), calls the stock artificially depressed, and tells investors not to focus on deliveries. Separately, he predicts about 30% of cars will be autonomous within 3-4 years.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Delivery numbers are the wrong metric under this thesis; the value sits in autonomy and robotics.
insights.quote: 30% of cars in the next 3 4 years are going to be autonomous

insights.claim: The host argues SpaceX went from a rocket launcher two years ago to an AI company that happens to have rockets, as its Q2 results show, building a full stack from launch and Starlink to space data centers, Grok AI, cars and humanoids. He says it launches one of every two rockets in the world and asks why it could not be a $100 trillion company.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano (host)
insights.so_what: This sizes the bull case for the combined entity at well above the $10 trillion figures in circulation.

insights.claim: Ives highlights Starlink as a competitive weapon in adjacent industries, for example airlines, where United's Starlink wifi could pull loyalty members away from Delta, and calls satellite data a major advantage because data is the new oil.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Starlink is a second-order disruptor for airlines and telecom carriers.

insights.claim: Ives says much of the market's nervousness comes from the midterms: a Democratic blue wave taking the House and Senate, with data-center moratorium talk from the party's left (AOC, Bernie), would at first blush be hugely negative for tech.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: A political tail risk to the AI capex trade around the midterm elections.

insights.claim: Ives argues political talk on data centers will differ from reality, because states that block them simply push the jobs and tax dollars to friendlier states, which limits how much a moratorium can actually slow the buildout.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Competition between states blunts the regulatory risk to the AI buildout.

insights.claim: Ives views the US as ahead of China in tech for the first time in 30 years, and says any US slowdown via regulation would make China the biggest winner. He calls the China market a picture of disaster over the last year.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: Geopolitics supports US AI policy staying permissive.

insights.claim: Ives reads the stock market rising after Fed Chair Warsh hiked rates as the Fed firing a shot across the bow the bond market was demanding, not as something that derails the AI cycle; he expects peace in the Middle East and an eventual move from hikes to holds to cuts over 12-18 months.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: A rate path that turns friendly would add to the AI earnings tailwind.

insights.claim: The host reports that legacy banks like JPMorgan are shutting off agent access while fintechs race to open up via MCPs; Robinhood and Coinbase now offer segregated accounts that agents can trade autonomously. He frames being pro-agent or anti-agent as what will separate winners from losers.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano (host)
insights.so_what: Fintechs that embrace agents may take share from incumbents that block them.
insights.quote: Robin Hood and Coinbase both have now like uh um kind of uh segregated accounts

insights.claim: Ives expects AI in investing to make markets more efficient and draw more investors in, while human judgment stays involved, though regulatory guardrails in finance set a high bar.
insights.speaker: Dan Ives
insights.so_what: A structural tailwind for brokers and platforms that enable AI-driven investing.

insights.claim: The host says his own companies have gone from using AI as a Google replacement six months ago to deploying it across video editing, coding, growth analytics and SEO, and expects the much larger group of late adopters to follow within five years.
insights.speaker: Anthony Pompliano (host)
insights.so_what: Enterprise adoption is still early, which suggests a long runway for AI demand.
